blocks.caption: Voltage is always measured as a difference between two points.

spans.text: A standard AA battery supplies about 1.5V. A USB port typically supplies 5V. These numbers tell you how much electrical push is available to drive current through whatever you connect.

blocks.text: A standard AA battery supplies about 1.5V. A USB port typically supplies 5V. These numbers tell you how much electrical push is available to drive current through whatever you connect.
Current — the flow

spans.text: Current is the actual rate of flow of electric charge through a circuit — continuing the water analogy, if voltage is the pressure, current is the amount of water actually moving through the pipe per second. Current is measured in amperes, usually shortened to amps or A. A small LED might draw around 20 milliamps (0.02A) to light up. A power tool motor might draw several amps under load.

blocks.text: Current is the actual rate of flow of electric charge through a circuit — continuing the water analogy, if voltage is the pressure, current is the amount of water actually moving through the pipe per second. Current is measured in amperes, usually shortened to amps or A. A small LED might draw around 20 milliamps (0.02A) to light up. A power tool motor might draw several amps under load.

blocks.caption: Current only flows through a complete, closed loop.

spans.text: Current only flows when there's a complete path — a closed loop — for it to travel around. Break the loop anywhere, even with a tiny gap, and current stops everywhere in that loop at once. That's the entire principle behind a switch: it's just a controlled gap you can open or close.

Resistance — the restriction

spans.text: Resistance is whatever in the circuit pushes back against that flow — again like a narrower section of pipe restricting how much water can get through even at the same pressure. Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). A thick, short wire has very low resistance. A long, thin wire — or a component specifically built to resist current, called a resistor — has higher resistance.

resistance where you need it — which turns out to matter constantly, because without resistance limiting it, current can rise to damaging levels almost instantly.

spans.text: Whenever you know any two of these three values, Ohm's Law gives you the third. This single relationship is the tool you'll reach for constantly — sizing a resistor, checking whether a component is safe to connect, or figuring out why a circuit isn't behaving the way you expected.

Putting it to work: sizing a resistor for an LED

spans.text: Here's where this becomes genuinely practical. Say you're powering an LED from a 5V source. The LED itself needs about 2V across it to work correctly, and it's rated to safely handle 20 milliamps (0.02A) of current. Connect it directly to 5V with no resistance in the way, and it will draw far more current than it's rated for — and burn out almost instantly.

Why this matters before you touch a sensor or motor

spans.text: Every sensor and motor you'll work with later in this course has voltage and current requirements, and getting those wrong is one of the most common ways beginners damage components. Supply too much voltage, and you can destroy a sensor instantly. Draw too much current through a component not rated for it, and it overheats or fails. Ohm's Law is the tool that lets you check these numbers before you connect anything, rather than finding out the hard way.

blocks.text: Lesson

spans.text: You now understand voltage, current, resistance, and how Ohm's Law ties them together. But so far you've only looked at the simplest possible circuit: one source, one component, one loop. Real circuits almost always involve multiple components, and how you connect them — in series or in parallel — completely changes how voltage and current behave across the whole circuit. Getting this wrong is one of the most common reasons a beginner's circuit doesn't do what they expected.

blocks.text: You now understand voltage, current, resistance, and how Ohm's Law ties them together. But so far you've only looked at the simplest possible circuit: one source, one component, one loop. Real circuits almost always involve multiple components, and how you connect them — in series or in parallel — completely changes how voltage and current behave across the whole circuit. Getting this wrong is one of the most common reasons a beginner's circuit doesn't do what they expected.
Series circuits: one path, shared current

spans.text: In a series circuit, components are connected one after another, forming a single path for current to flow. There's only one route, so the same current flows through every component in that loop — current doesn't get "used up" or split along the way.

blocks.text: In a series circuit, components are connected one after another, forming a single path for current to flow. There's only one route, so the same current flows through every component in that loop — current doesn't get "used up" or split along the way.

blocks.caption: The same current flows through every component along a single series path.

spans.text: Voltage behaves differently. The source voltage gets divided up across the components in the loop, in proportion to each component's resistance. If you add up the voltage across every component in a series circuit, it always equals the total source voltage — nothing is lost, it's just distributed.

blocks.text: Voltage behaves differently. The source voltage gets divided up across the components in the loop, in proportion to each component's resistance. If you add up the voltage across every component in a series circuit, it always equals the total source voltage — nothing is lost, it's just distributed.

blocks.caption: Voltage splits across series components but always sums back to the source voltage.

spans.text: This is exactly what you saw in the LED and resistor example from Topic 2.1, without naming it yet: the 5V source split into 3V across the resistor and 2V across the LED, because they were connected in series, sharing one path and one current.

blocks.text: This is exactly what you saw in the LED and resistor example from Topic 2.1, without naming it yet: the 5V source split into 3V across the resistor and 2V across the LED, because they were connected in series, sharing one path and one current.
Series circuits: the single point of failure

spans.text: Because there's only one path, series circuits have a real weakness: if any single component fails open (stops conducting), the entire loop breaks, and current stops everywhere in the circuit at once — not just at the failed component. This is the classic old-style string of holiday lights where one dead bulb takes out the whole strand.

blocks.text: Because there's only one path, series circuits have a real weakness: if any single component fails open (stops conducting), the entire loop breaks, and current stops everywhere in the circuit at once — not just at the failed component. This is the classic old-style string of holiday lights where one dead bulb takes out the whole strand.

blocks.caption: One failed component is enough to stop current everywhere in a series loop.

spans.text: That weakness is sometimes intentional, though — a fuse is designed to be the deliberate weak point in a series path, breaking the circuit on purpose if current gets dangerously high.

blocks.text: That weakness is sometimes intentional, though — a fuse is designed to be the deliberate weak point in a series path, breaking the circuit on purpose if current gets dangerously high.
Parallel circuits: multiple paths, shared voltage

spans.text: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points, each forming its own separate path back to the source. Voltage behaves simply here: every component in parallel sees the exact same voltage, because they're all connected across the same two points.

blocks.text: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across the same two points, each forming its own separate path back to the source. Voltage behaves simply here: every component in parallel sees the exact same voltage, because they're all connected across the same two points.

blocks.caption: Every branch in a parallel circuit sees the same voltage.

spans.text: Current behaves the opposite way from series: the total current from the source splits across the different paths, with each path carrying current in proportion to how much resistance it has. Add up the current through every parallel path, and it equals the total current leaving the source.

blocks.text: Current behaves the opposite way from series: the total current from the source splits across the different paths, with each path carrying current in proportion to how much resistance it has. Add up the current through every parallel path, and it equals the total current leaving the source.

blocks.caption: Branch currents in a parallel circuit add up to the total current from the source.

blocks.text: Parallel circuits: independence between branches

spans.text: This is the practical advantage of parallel wiring: if one component in a parallel branch fails open, current simply stops flowing through that one branch — every other branch keeps working normally, because
each has its own separate path back to the source.

blocks.text: This is the practical advantage of parallel wiring: if one component in a parallel branch fails open, current simply stops flowing through that one branch — every other branch keeps working normally, because each has its own separate path back to the source.

blocks.caption: A failed branch in a parallel circuit doesn't affect the others.

spans.text: This is why household electrical wiring is parallel: one dead light bulb in your room doesn't take out every other outlet and light in the house.

blocks.text: This is why household electrical wiring is parallel: one dead light bulb in your room doesn't take out every other outlet and light in the house.
Why this distinction matters for component design

spans.text: This isn't just circuit theory — it directly affects decisions you'll make building real systems. Wiring multiple LEDs in series means they all share one current path, so if you're running them from a fixed-current source, each LED gets the same current, but the voltage needed from your source grows with every LED added. Wiring the same LEDs in parallel means each one sees full source voltage independently, but now your source needs to supply enough total current for all of them combined, and a single weak LED drawing more than its share can pull current away from the others.

Wiring multiple LEDs in series means they all share one current path, so if you're running them from a fixed-current source, each LED gets the same current, but the voltage needed from your source grows with every LED added. Wiring the same LEDs in parallel means each one sees full source voltage independently, but now your source needs to supply enough total current for all of them combined, and a single weak LED drawing more than its share can pull current away from the others.

spans.text: Neither arrangement is universally "better" — which one you choose depends entirely on what your source can supply and what behavior you actually want from the circuit.

A quick way to tell them apart by eye

blocks.caption: Series components form one line; parallel components branch and rejoin.

spans.text: When you're looking at a circuit diagram, series components sit along one continuous line, like beads on a single string. Parallel components branch off the same two points and rejoin on the other side, like several lanes on a highway that all start and end at the same two junctions. Most real circuits you'll encounter later in this course combine both — some sections in series, some in parallel — so being able to recognize each pattern at a glance is a skill worth building now, before the circuits get more complex.

Most real circuits you'll encounter later in this course combine both — some sections in series, some in parallel — so being able to recognize each pattern at a glance is a skill worth building now, before the circuits get more complex.
Where this leaves you

spans.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify whether a given circuit arrangement is series or parallel, predict how voltage and current will behave in each case, and explain why a component failure affects a series circuit very differently than a parallel one. Next, you'll move from circuit arrangement to the individual building blocks themselves — resistors, capacitors, diodes, and transistors — the essential components you'll be wiring into both kinds of circuits throughout the rest of this course.

spans.text: You now understand how components connect — series and parallel — and the three quantities that describe what's happening in a circuit. This lesson introduces the components themselves: four parts that show up in almost every circuit you'll ever build. You've already met one of them. The other three are new, and each does something the other three can't.

This lesson introduces the components themselves: four parts that show up in almost every circuit you'll ever build. You've already met one of them. The other three are new, and each does something the other three can't.
Resistors — controlling current

spans.text: You already know what a resistor does from Topic 2.1: it adds a known, controlled amount of resistance to a circuit, limiting current to a safe level. Resistors are color-coded with bands that tell you their resistance value — a skill worth building early, since you won't always have a multimeter handy to check.

blocks.text: You already know what a resistor does from Topic 2.1: it adds a known, controlled amount of resistance to a circuit, limiting current to a safe level. Resistors are color-coded with bands that tell you their resistance value — a skill worth building early, since you won't always have a multimeter handy to check.

blocks.caption: Color bands on a resistor encode its resistance value and tolerance.

spans.text: Resistors are non-polarized, meaning they work the same way no matter which direction current flows through them. You can install one backwards and it behaves identically. That's not true for every component on this list.

blocks.text: Resistors are non-polarized, meaning they work the same way no matter which direction current flows through them. You can install one backwards and it behaves identically. That's not true for every component on this list.
Capacitors — storing and releasing charge

spans.text: A capacitor stores electrical charge temporarily, then releases it when needed. Picture it like a small, fast-charging reservoir: it fills up with charge while voltage is applied, and discharges that stored charge back into the circuit when voltage drops or the capacitor is connected across a path.

blocks.text: A capacitor stores electrical charge temporarily, then releases it when needed. Picture it like a small, fast-charging reservoir: it fills up with charge while voltage is applied, and discharges that stored charge back into the circuit when voltage drops or the capacitor is connected across a path.

blocks.caption: A capacitor filling with charge, then releasing it back into the circuit.

spans.text: This storage behavior makes capacitors useful in a few recurring roles. They smooth out power supply fluctuations by filling in small dips in voltage. They filter unwanted electrical noise out of a signal. And they can introduce a brief time delay in a circuit, since charging or discharging isn't instant — it takes a small, predictable amount of time.

blocks.text: This storage behavior makes capacitors useful in a few recurring roles. They smooth out power supply fluctuations by filling in small dips in voltage. They filter unwanted electrical noise out of a signal. And they can introduce a brief time delay in a circuit, since charging or discharging isn't instant — it takes a small, predictable amount of time.

blocks.caption: A polarized capacitor's positive and negative leads matter.

spans.text: Some capacitors are polarized, meaning they have a distinct positive and negative terminal, and connecting one backwards can damage the component or the circuit it's in. Always check before wiring one in — polarized capacitors are usually clearly marked with a stripe or a longer lead on the positive side.

blocks.text: Some capacitors are polarized, meaning they have a distinct positive and negative terminal, and connecting one backwards can damage the component or the circuit it's in. Always check before wiring one in — polarized capacitors are usually clearly marked with a stripe or a longer lead on the positive side.
Diodes — one-way valves for current

spans.text: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction and blocks it in the other. Think of it as a one-way valve for electricity: current flows freely one way, and hits a wall going the other way.

blocks.text: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction and blocks it in the other. Think of it as a one-way valve for electricity: current flows freely one way, and hits a wall going the other way.

blocks.caption: Current flows freely one direction through a diode, and is blocked the other.

spans.text: This makes diodes essential for protecting circuits from reversed connections — if someone (including you, on a bad day) connects a battery backwards, a correctly placed diode can prevent current from flowing the wrong way through sensitive components, protecting them from damage.

blocks.text: This makes diodes essential for protecting circuits from reversed connections — if someone (including you, on a bad day) connects a battery backwards, a correctly placed diode can prevent current from flowing the wrong way through sensitive components, protecting them from damage.

blocks.caption: An LED is a diode that happens to emit light when current flows the correct way.

spans.text: Diodes are also the basis of how an LED works: an LED is simply a diode that happens to emit light when current flows through it in the correct direction, which is exactly why LEDs only light up one way around.

blocks.text: Diodes are also the basis of how an LED works: an LED is simply a diode that happens to emit light when current flows through it in the correct direction, which is exactly why LEDs only light up one way around.

spans.text: Diodes are always polarized — direction matters completely. Install one backwards, and at best it simply blocks current entirely; at worst, depending on the circuit, it can fail or damage other components.

blocks.text: Diodes are always polarized — direction matters completely. Install one backwards, and at best it simply blocks current entirely; at worst, depending on the circuit, it can fail or damage other components.
Transistors — the switch that controls itself

spans.text: A transistor acts as an electronically controlled switch, but with an important difference from a simple mechanical switch: instead of a person flipping it, a small signal controls whether a much larger current is allowed to flow. A tiny current or voltage on one terminal determines whether the transistor allows current to pass between its other two terminals.

blocks.text: A transistor acts as an electronically controlled switch, but with an important difference from a simple mechanical switch: instead of a person flipping it, a small signal controls whether a much larger current is allowed to flow. A tiny current or voltage on one terminal determines whether the transistor allows current to pass between its other two terminals.

blocks.caption: A small control signal determines whether a much larger current flows.

spans.text: This is the property that makes transistors so powerful: a small signal — like the output from a microcontroller — can control something requiring far more current than the microcontroller could ever supply directly, such as a motor or a bright light. The microcontroller doesn't power the motor itself; it tells the transistor to allow power to the motor.

blocks.text: This is the property that makes transistors so powerful: a small signal — like the output from a microcontroller — can control something requiring far more current than the microcontroller could ever supply directly, such as a motor or a bright light. The microcontroller doesn't power the motor itself; it tells the transistor to allow power to the motor.

blocks.caption: A microcontroller's small signal telling a transistor to power a motor.

spans.text: Transistors have three terminals, and getting the right terminal connected to the right part of the circuit matters — unlike a resistor, you can't just connect it any way and expect it to work.

blocks.text: Transistors have three terminals, and getting the right terminal connected to the right part of the circuit matters — unlike a resistor, you can't just connect it any way and expect it to work.
Why these four, specifically

spans.text: These four components recur constantly because each one does something fundamentally different, and most real circuits need some combination of all four: resistors to control current levels, capacitors to store charge and smooth behavior over time, diodes to enforce one-way current flow, and transistors to let a small signal control something larger. Once you start reading circuit diagrams for sensors and motors later in this course, you'll recognize these four everywhere — often working together in the same small section of a circuit.

topics.title: Reading Datasheets and Using a Multimeter

blocks.text: Reading Datasheets and Using a Multimeter

spans.text: Every component you've met so far, resistors, capacitors, diodes and transistors, has a limit. Push a resistor past its power rating and it cooks. Feed a transistor more current than it can take and it dies, often silently, and you spend two hours debugging code that was never the problem. Two skills protect you from this: knowing what a component is rated for, and knowing what your circuit is actually doing. The first comes from the datasheet. The second comes from the multimeter.

blocks.caption: When a circuit fails, check the hardware before you blame the code.

blocks.text: What a datasheet is

spans.text: A datasheet is the manufacturer's official statement of what a component does and what it can survive. It is written by the people who built the part, so it settles any argument about how it behaves. Tutorials, forum posts and blog articles can be wrong. The datasheet is the primary source, and you find it by searching the part number followed by “datasheet”.

spans.text: Datasheets look intimidating because they are dense, but nearly all of them follow the same structure, and you only need a few sections.

blocks.text: Datasheets look intimidating because they are dense, but nearly all of them follow the same structure, and you only need a few sections.

blocks.caption: The six sections of a typical datasheet. Absolute Maximum Ratings (highlighted) is the one you must never skip.

spans.text: The first page
gives a one-paragraph description of the part, a feature list, and usually a pinout diagram. Read this first to confirm you have the right component for the job.

blocks.text: The first page gives a one-paragraph description of the part, a feature list, and usually a pinout diagram. Read this first to confirm you have the right component for the job.

spans.text: The pinout

shows which pin is which. This matters more than it sounds. A transistor has three legs, and the same package can have its legs arranged differently across manufacturers. Wiring the collector where the emitter should go is one of the most common beginner mistakes, and the pinout prevents it. Note also that pinout diagrams are drawn from the top or bottom of the part, and the sheet says which.

blocks.caption: The same transistor drawn from two viewpoints. The leg order flips between views, so always check which view the datasheet uses.

spans.text: Absolute maximum ratings

are the limits you must never exceed. For a typical small-signal NPN transistor, this table might list a maximum collector current of around 800 mA, a maximum collector-emitter voltage of around 40 V, and a maximum power dissipation of a few hundred milliwatts. These figures are illustrative, typical of this kind of part rather than taken from one specific datasheet. They are not operating targets. They are the edge of the cliff. A good habit is to design so you stay well under them, commonly at half or less of the maximum, to leave margin for heat, supply fluctuations and mistakes.

spans.text: Electrical characteristics

are the values the part actually delivers under stated test conditions. For a transistor, this includes its current gain, the voltage drop when it is fully switched on, and how quickly it switches. Read the conditions printed next to each value. A gain figure measured at 10 mA collector current may be very different at 500 mA. Beginners often quote a number from the table without noticing it was measured under conditions that don't match their circuit.

spans.text: Typical, minimum and maximum columns.

Many values appear in three columns. Typical is what you'll usually see. Minimum and maximum are the guaranteed bounds across manufacturing variation. When you are designing something that must work reliably, design against the worst case, not the typical one. If the gain is guaranteed to be at least 100 and typically 200, build the circuit so it works at 100.

spans.text: Graphs and package drawings

come last. The graphs show how behavior changes with temperature and current, which is useful once you start pushing a part. The package drawing gives physical dimensions, which matters when you design a PCB or a 3D-printed mount.

spans.text: A practical way to read an unfamiliar datasheet: confirm the part type on page one, check the pinout, check the absolute maximum ratings against your circuit, then read the electrical characteristics for the specific values your design depends on. Everything else you can leave until you need it.

What a multimeter measures

spans.text: A multimeter is the tool that tells you what is really happening in a circuit, as opposed to what you think is happening. It has two probes, a red one and a black one, and a dial that selects what you are measuring. The functions you will use constantly are these.

blocks.text: A multimeter is the tool that tells you what is really happening in a circuit, as opposed to what you think is happening. It has two probes, a red one and a black one, and a dial that selects what you are measuring. The functions you will use constantly are these.

blocks.caption: A handheld multimeter and its main dial positions. Note the separate mA jack, used only for current.

spans.text: DC voltage.

Set the dial to DC voltage (marked V with a straight line above a dashed line). Touch the black probe to the ground side and the red probe to the point you want to measure. Voltage is measured across two points, so the meter goes in parallel with whatever you are examining. This is the measurement you will take most often: Is the battery actually 3.7 V? Is the sensor receiving 5 V? Is the motor driver output reaching the motor?

blocks.text: DC voltage. Set the dial to DC voltage (marked V with a straight line above a dashed line). Touch the black probe to the ground side and the red probe to the point you want to measure. Voltage is measured across two points, so the meter goes in parallel with whatever you are examining. This is the measurement you will take most often: Is the battery actually 3.7 V? Is the sensor receiving 5 V? Is the motor driver output reaching the motor?

spans.text: Resistance.

Set the dial to ohms (marked with the Greek letter omega). The meter sends a tiny current through the component and calculates resistance from the result. Two rules matter. First, power must be off, or the circuit's own voltage will give you a wrong reading and can damage the meter. Second, for an accurate reading, the component should ideally be out of the circuit, because other parts connected in parallel will skew the result.

blocks.text: Resistance. Set the dial to ohms (marked with the Greek letter omega). The meter sends a tiny current through the component and calculates resistance from the result. Two rules matter. First, power must be off, or the circuit's own voltage will give you a wrong reading and can damage the meter. Second, for an accurate reading, the component should ideally be out of the circuit, because other parts connected in parallel will skew the result.

spans.text: Continuity.

This setting, usually marked with a sound-wave or diode-like symbol, beeps when there is a low-resistance path between the probes. It is the fastest way to check whether a wire is broken, a solder joint is good, or two pins that should not be connected are accidentally shorted together. Like resistance, it should only be used with power off.

blocks.text: Continuity. This setting, usually marked with a sound-wave or diode-like symbol, beeps when there is a low-resistance path between the probes. It is the fastest way to check whether a wire is broken, a solder joint is good, or two pins that should not be connected are accidentally shorted together. Like resistance, it should only be used with power off.

spans.text: Current.

Measuring current is where beginners get hurt. To measure current, the meter must become part of the circuit, in series, so the current flows through it. That means you break the circuit and insert the meter into the gap. Current measurement also uses a different input jack on most meters, often marked mA or A. If you leave the red probe in the current jack and then touch it across a voltage source, you create a near-short circuit through the meter, which blows its internal fuse at best. Make it a habit to return the red probe to the voltage jack immediately after any current measurement.

Make it a habit to return the red probe to the voltage jack immediately after any current measurement.

blocks.caption: Voltage is measured across a component (parallel). Current is measured through the meter (series).

spans.text: Diode test.

This mode checks diodes and also LEDs and transistor junctions. A working silicon diode typically shows a forward voltage around 0.6 to 0.7 V in one direction and no reading in the other. This is a quick way to confirm a component is the right way round, or whether it has failed.

blocks.text: Diode test. This mode checks diodes and also LEDs and transistor junctions. A working silicon diode typically shows a forward voltage around 0.6 to 0.7 V in one direction and no reading in the other. This is a quick way to confirm a component is the right way round, or whether it has failed.
A worked example: putting both skills together

spans.text: Suppose you want to switch a small DC motor from a microcontroller using a transistor. The datasheet for your transistor lists a maximum collector current of 800 mA. You measure the motor's running current with the meter in series and read 250 mA. That is comfortably under the limit, at roughly a third of it, so the transistor is a reasonable choice. You then measure the stall current, which means briefly holding the motor shaft still, and read 900 mA. Now you know the transistor would be overloaded if the motor ever jams. The datasheet told you the limit and the multimeter told you the real demand, and together they showed a problem before anything burned. The fix is to choose a transistor, or a motor driver, with a higher rating.

blocks.text: Safety habits worth building now

spans.text: Turn the power off before measuring resistance or checking continuity. Start on a higher range if your meter is manual, and work down. Never measure current across a voltage source. Keep your fingers behind the probe guards. And never use a hobby-grade meter on mains electricity unless it is rated for it. Mains voltage can kill, and it is outside the scope of anything you will build in this course.

Where this leaves you

spans.text: You now have the two habits that separate someone who guesses from someone who engineers: check the rating before you build, and measure the result after. That completes Module 2. You understand voltage, current and resistance, how series and parallel circuits behave, what the essential components do, and how to verify all of it on a real bench. Next comes Module 3, where we move from powering circuits to sensing the world with them, starting with the question of what a sensor actually is and how analog and digital signals differ.

topics.title: What Is a Sensor? Analog vs. Digital Signals

blocks.text: What Is a Sensor? Analog vs. Digital Signals

spans.text: A microcontroller is excellent at arithmetic and completely blind to the world. It has no idea whether an oven is at 20 °C or 200 °C, whether a robot arm has reached the end of its travel, or whether a generator shaft is shaking itself apart. Everything it will ever know about the physical world arrives as an electrical signal, and something has to produce that signal. That something is a sensor.

blocks.text: A microcontroller is excellent at arithmetic and completely blind to the world. It has no idea whether an oven is at 20 °C or 200 °C, whether a robot arm has reached the end of its travel, or whether a generator shaft is shaking itself apart. Everything it will ever know about the physical world arrives as an electrical signal, and something has to produce that signal. That something is a sensor.

blocks.caption: Without a sensor the controller is blind. With one, it knows what the physical world is doing.

blocks.text: What a sensor is

spans.text: A sensor is a device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal that a circuit can read. The quantity might be temperature, force, light, position, speed, pressure or vibration. The signal is usually a voltage, though it can also be a current, a resistance, or a stream of digital data.

blocks.text: A sensor is a device that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal that a circuit can read. The quantity might be temperature, force, light, position, speed, pressure or vibration. The signal is usually a voltage, though it can also be a current, a resistance, or a stream of digital data.

spans.text: Inside most sensors, a sensing element changes some electrical property when the physical quantity changes. A thermistor changes its resistance as it heats up. A strain gauge changes its resistance as it stretches. A photodiode changes its output as light falls on it. A small circuit then turns that change into something your controller can use, most often a voltage. You will also hear the word transducer, which means any device that converts one form of energy into another. A sensor is a transducer whose output is electrical.

blocks.text: Inside most sensors, a sensing element changes some electrical property when the physical quantity changes. A thermistor changes its resistance as it heats up. A strain gauge changes its resistance as it stretches. A photodiode changes its output as light falls on it. A small circuit then turns that change into something your controller can use, most often a voltage. You will also hear the word transducer, which means any device that converts one form of energy into another. A sensor is a transducer whose output is electrical.

blocks.caption: A sensor translates a physical quantity into an electrical signal the controller can read.

spans.text: This has a consequence worth holding onto. A sensor never hands you a temperature. It hands you a voltage that you convert into a temperature using what the datasheet tells you about the relationship. Every sensor reading is an electrical measurement that your software interprets.

blocks.text: This has a consequence worth holding onto. A sensor never hands you a temperature. It hands you a voltage that you convert into a temperature using what the datasheet tells you about the relationship. Every sensor reading is an electrical measurement that your software interprets.
Where sensors sit in a mechatronic system

spans.text: Every mechatronic system follows the same loop: sense, think, act. Take an industrial oven. A temperature sensor reports the current temperature, the microcontroller compares it to the target, and a heater switches on or off to close the gap. The sensor is the first link. Without it, the controller is guessing, and a controller that guesses is just a timer. Module 4 covers the actuators at the other end of the loop. This module is about the sensing end.

A temperature sensor reports the current temperature, the microcontroller compares it to the target, and a heater switches on or off to close the gap. The sensor is the first link. Without it, the controller is guessing, and a controller that guesses is just a timer. Module 4 covers the actuators at the other end of the loop. This module is about the sensing end.

blocks.caption: The sense-think-act loop in an oven. This module focuses on the first link, sensing.

blocks.text: Two kinds of signal

spans.text: A signal is a quantity that carries information as it changes over time. Sensors produce two kinds, and the difference decides how you wire them, read them and trust them.

blocks.text: A signal is a quantity that carries information as it changes over time. Sensors produce two kinds, and the difference decides how you wire them, read them and trust them.

spans.text: Analog signals

can take any value within a range, and they vary smoothly. Consider a temperature sensor that outputs about 10 millivolts for every degree Celsius, which is how some common sensors work. At 20 °C it outputs 0.200 V. At 20.5 °C it outputs 0.205 V. At 20.51 °C it outputs 0.2051 V. There is no gap between possible values. A potentiometer attached to a robot joint behaves the same way: its output voltage follows the joint angle continuously. Analog signals carry rich information, and the sensors producing them are often simple. Their weakness is noise. Small unwanted voltage variations picked up along the wire add error that you cannot easily separate from the real signal, and a long wire running through a noisy factory makes it worse.

Consider a temperature sensor that outputs about 10 millivolts for every degree Celsius, which is how some common sensors work. At 20 °C it outputs 0.200 V. At 20.5 °C it outputs 0.205 V. At 20.51 °C it outputs 0.2051 V. There is no gap between possible values. A potentiometer attached to a robot joint behaves the same way: its output voltage follows the joint angle continuously. Analog signals carry rich information, and the sensors producing them are often simple. Their weakness is noise. Small unwanted voltage variations picked up along the wire add error that you cannot easily separate from the real signal, and a long wire running through a noisy factory makes it worse.

blocks.caption: An analog signal can take any value in its range. The 10 mV per degree figure is illustrative.

spans.text: Digital signals

take only two values: high or low, on or off, 1 or 0. On a typical microcontroller, high is close to the supply voltage, commonly 3.3 V or 5 V, and low is close to 0 V. A limit switch at the end of a conveyor is a good example: either the part has arrived and pressed it, or it has not. Digital signals are robust, because noise has to be large enough to push the voltage across the threshold between low and high before it causes an error. The cost is information. One wire carries one yes-or-no answer.

A limit switch at the end of a conveyor is a good example: either the part has arrived and pressed it, or it has not. Digital signals are robust, because noise has to be large enough to push the voltage across the threshold between low and high before it causes an error. The cost is information. One wire carries one yes-or-no answer.

blocks.caption: A digital signal has two states. Noise must cross the threshold to cause an error.

spans.text: The word digital also covers a second kind of sensor. Many modern sensors contain their own small electronics that measure, convert and then send the result as a number, as a stream of high and low pulses following an agreed communication protocol. You will use these in Topic 3.3. The distinction to keep clear is between a digital on/off signal, which is a single two-state wire, and a digital data sensor, which sends actual measurements as numbers.

Many modern sensors contain their own small electronics that measure, convert and then send the result as a number, as a stream of high and low pulses following an agreed communication protocol. You will use these in Topic 3.3. The distinction to keep clear is between a digital on/off signal, which is a single two-state wire, and a digital data sensor, which sends actual measurements as numbers.
Turning analog into numbers: the ADC

spans.text: A microcontroller's processor works with numbers, so an analog voltage has to be converted before your code can use it. The circuit that does this is the analog-to-digital converter, or ADC. It measures the voltage at one instant and reports it as a whole number. Two figures define how well it does that.

blocks.text: A microcontroller's processor works with numbers, so an analog voltage has to be converted before your code can use it. The circuit that does this is the analog-to-digital converter, or ADC. It measures the voltage at one instant and reports it as a whole number. Two figures define how well it does that.

spans.text: Resolution

is the number of bits the ADC uses. An n-bit ADC can report 2 to the power n different values. A 10-bit ADC reports 1,024 levels, numbered 0 to 1,023. If it spans 0 to 5 V, each step is about 4.9 mV. Any change smaller than one step is invisible to it.

blocks.text: Resolution is the number of bits the ADC uses. An n-bit ADC can report 2 to the power n different values. A 10-bit ADC reports 1,024 levels, numbered 0 to 1,023. If it spans 0 to 5 V, each step is about 4.9 mV. Any change smaller than one step is invisible to it.

spans.text: Sampling rate
is how often the ADC takes a reading. The faster the quantity changes, the faster you must sample. A slow oven needs a reading every second. A vibrating generator shaft needs thousands per second.

blocks.text: Sampling rate is how often the ADC takes a reading. The faster the quantity changes, the faster you must sample. A slow oven needs a reading every second. A vibrating generator shaft needs thousands per second.

blocks.caption: A 10-bit ADC turns a smooth signal into 1,024 discrete steps.

blocks.text: A worked example

spans.text: Suppose the temperature sensor above, at 10 mV per °C, feeds a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V range. The room is exactly 35.0 °C, so the sensor outputs 0.350 V. The ADC computes 0.350 divided by 5, multiplied by 1,024, which is 71.68. It reports whole numbers, so your code receives 71.

blocks.text: Suppose the temperature sensor above, at 10 mV per °C, feeds a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V range. The room is exactly 35.0 °C, so the sensor outputs 0.350 V. The ADC computes 0.350 divided by 5, multiplied by 1,024, which is 71.68. It reports whole numbers, so your code receives 71.

spans.text: To convert back, your code multiplies 71 by 5/1,024, which gives 0.3467 V, and divides by 10 mV per °C. The result is 34.67 °C. That is not a fault. It is the resolution limit at work. Each ADC step

here equals about 0.49 °C, so this setup cannot tell 35.0 °C from 34.8 °C. If your application needs to see changes of 0.1 °C, you need a higher-resolution ADC, or you amplify the sensor signal before it reaches the ADC so each degree covers more steps.

blocks.caption: From sensor to ADC to code: the reading lands on 34.67 °C because of the resolution limit.

blocks.text: Choosing between them

spans.text: Use an analog sensor when you need a continuous measurement, such as temperature, position or pressure, and your controller has an ADC. Use a digital on/off sensor when the question is a plain yes or no: is the door closed, did the part arrive, has the arm reached its limit. Use a digital data sensor when you want precision and noise immunity and your controller supports its protocol.

blocks.text: Use an analog sensor when you need a continuous measurement, such as temperature, position or pressure, and your controller has an ADC. Use a digital on/off sensor when the question is a plain yes or no: is the door closed, did the part arrive, has the arm reached its limit. Use a digital data sensor when you want precision and noise immunity and your controller supports its protocol.
What to check before you pick a sensor

spans.text: Four specifications matter on every sensor datasheet, which is where the skill from Topic 2.4 pays off.
Range
is the span the sensor can measure.
Resolution
is the smallest change it can show.
Accuracy
is how close its reading is to the true value.
Response time
is how quickly the output follows a change. Resolution and accuracy are not the same thing. A sensor can display values in steps of 0.01 degrees and still be wrong by 2 degrees.

Where this leaves you

spans.text: You now know what a sensor really does: it converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, and your software turns that signal back into meaning. You can tell analog signals from digital ones, you know why an ADC limits how finely you can read an analog sensor, and you have four specifications to check before choosing one. blocks.text: Common Sensor Types

spans.text: Open any supplier's catalogue and you will find hundreds of sensors. They look different, but they sort quickly once you ask two questions. What physical quantity does it measure? And what kind of signal does it give back? The first question tells you which family it belongs to. The second, from Topic 3.1, tells you how to wire it and read it.

And what kind of signal does it give back? The first question tells you which family it belongs to. The second, from Topic 3.1, tells you how to wire it and read it.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of sensors, six families. The trick is knowing which question to ask first.

The part names are examples of each type, not recommendations. When you build, the datasheet for the exact part in your hand is the final word.

blocks.text: Resistive sensors: a note before we start

spans.text: Several sensors never output a voltage at all. A thermistor, a photoresistor and a force-sensitive resistor all change their resistance. A microcontroller reads voltage, not resistance, so you convert one into the other with a voltage divider, the same circuit you met in Module 2.

blocks.text: Several sensors never output a voltage at all. A thermistor, a photoresistor and a force-sensitive resistor all change their resistance. A microcontroller reads voltage, not resistance, so you convert one into the other with a voltage divider, the same circuit you met in Module 2.

spans.text: Put a thermistor in series with a 10 kΩ fixed resistor across 5 V, and read the voltage at the junction between them. A “10k” thermistor is 10 kΩ at 25 °C, so at room temperature the junction sits at 2.5 V and a 10-bit ADC reports 512. Warm it up until its resistance falls to 5 kΩ and the junction rises to 3.33 V, an ADC reading of 682. The resistance changed, the divider turned that into a voltage, and the ADC turned the voltage into a number. Swap the two resistors and the voltage moves the opposite way, so always work out which direction your wiring gives.

blocks.text: Temperature

spans.text: The
NTC thermistor

is cheap, small and fast. NTC means its resistance falls as temperature rises. The catch is that the change is not a straight line, so your software converts resistance to temperature with an equation from the datasheet, usually the B-parameter equation. Thermistors that are both labeled “10k” can carry different constants depending on the manufacturer, so use the numbers for your exact part.

blocks.text: The NTC thermistor is cheap, small and fast. NTC means its resistance falls as temperature rises. The catch is that the change is not a straight line, so your software converts resistance to temperature with an equation from the datasheet, usually the B-parameter equation. Thermistors that are both labeled “10k” can carry different constants depending on the manufacturer, so use the numbers for your exact part.

spans.text: The
LM35

gives an analog voltage of 10 mV per °C, so 25 °C reads 0.250 V. It is linear and the simplest temperature sensor to use. Check its supply range before you choose it: it needs roughly 4 V or more, so it is a poor fit for a board that runs at 3.3 V. Measuring below freezing needs extra circuitry.

blocks.text: The LM35 gives an analog voltage of 10 mV per °C, so 25 °C reads 0.250 V. It is linear and the simplest temperature sensor to use. Check its supply range before you choose it: it needs roughly 4 V or more, so it is a poor fit for a board that runs at 3.3 V. Measuring below freezing needs extra circuitry.

spans.text: The
DS18B20

sends temperature as digital data over a single wire, using a protocol called 1-Wire. It is accurate to about half a degree across the middle of its range, and you can choose between 9 and 12 bits of resolution. It will not communicate at all unless a 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor connects the data line to the supply. Counterfeit chips are common and often less accurate, so buy from a reputable source.

blocks.caption: Three ways to read temperature: a resistance, an analog voltage, and digital data.

spans.text: A
thermocouple

is two different metals joined at a tip. It produces a tiny voltage, tens of microvolts per degree, that depends on the temperature difference between the tip and the board end. Reading that directly needs careful amplification and compensation for the board end's own temperature, which is why thermocouples are usually paired with an interface chip that reports the temperature digitally. Use one when other sensors would melt, such as furnaces, kilns and exhaust systems, where some probes work well above 1,000 °C. The right interface chip depends on your temperature range and supply voltage, so check its datasheet.

Light

spans.text: A
photoresistor

, or LDR, drops in resistance as light increases. It is cheap and good for answering “is it light or dark?” It responds slowly, in tens of milliseconds, and it is not calibrated, so it cannot give you a trustworthy lux figure. Two LDRs with different part numbers can behave very differently.

blocks.text: A photoresistor, or LDR, drops in resistance as light increases. It is cheap and good for answering “is it light or dark?” It responds slowly, in tens of milliseconds, and it is not calibrated, so it cannot give you a trustworthy lux figure. Two LDRs with different part numbers can behave very differently.

spans.text: The

reports illuminance in lux directly, as digital data over I2C. Its resolution is about 1 lux, though its accuracy is only within tens of percent, which is plenty to tell bright from dim and not enough for lab work. The bare chip is a 3.3 V part, and many breakout boards add a regulator, so check what yours includes. A pin on the chip selects one of two addresses, so two sensors can share the same bus.

Distance

spans.text: The
ultrasonic sensor

(the common HC-SR04 type) sends out a burst of sound and times the echo. Its output is a digital pulse whose width is proportional to the distance. Sound travels about 343 m/s in room-temperature air, and the pulse covers the trip out and back, so distance equals pulse time multiplied by 343, divided by 2. An echo pulse of 5.8 ms means about 1 m. The usable
range is roughly 2 cm to 4 m. Closer than the minimum, readings are unreliable. Soft surfaces such as fabric and foam absorb the sound, and surfaces at a steep angle bounce it away from the sensor.

spans.text: There is one wiring trap. This sensor runs on 5 V and its echo pin outputs 5 V, which can damage the pin of a 3.3 V controller. A divider of 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ brings it down to 3.33 V.

spans.text: The
Sharp infrared distance sensor

(the GP2Y0A21YK0F type) outputs an analog voltage that falls as the object gets farther, over a range of roughly 10 to 80 cm. The curve is not a straight line, so you convert voltage to distance using a curve or formula fitted to the datasheet graph. Its trap is the minimum range. Inside it, the output drops, so an object placed very close can look as though it is far away.

spans.text: The
VL53L0X

is a laser time-of-flight sensor that reports distance in millimetres as digital data over I2C. It reaches about 2 m. Its accuracy depends on how reflective the target is and on ambient light, so test it against your real target.

Motion and orientation

spans.text: A
PIR sensor

(the HC-SR501 type) detects changes in infrared radiation, such as a warm body moving across its view. Its output is a plain on/off signal, and it reaches several metres across a wide cone. It takes about a minute to settle after power-up, and once triggered it holds its output for a set time. It detects movement, not a person standing still.

blocks.text: A PIR sensor (the HC-SR501 type) detects changes in infrared radiation, such as a warm body moving across its view. Its output is a plain on/off signal, and it reaches several metres across a wide cone. It takes about a minute to settle after power-up, and once triggered it holds its output for a set time. It detects movement, not a person standing still.

spans.text: The

is an inertial sensor that combines a three-axis accelerometer with a three-axis gyroscope, reporting digital data over I2C. The ranges are selectable, from ±2 g to ±16 g for acceleration and from ±250 to ±2,000 degrees per second for rotation. The gyroscope reports how fast something is rotating, so you get an angle by adding up those readings over time, and tiny errors add up with them. That slow build-up is called drift. The accelerometer can give tilt from gravity but is noisy and gets confused when the device itself moves. Real systems combine the two with a filter. These sensors are widely used to watch tilt and vibration on machinery.

Position

spans.text: A
potentiometer

gives an analog voltage that follows the shaft angle, which makes it a simple absolute angle sensor. It rotates roughly 300 degrees, with dead zones at the ends, and forcing it past its end stop can break the wiper.

blocks.text: A potentiometer gives an analog voltage that follows the shaft angle, which makes it a simple absolute angle sensor. It rotates roughly 300 degrees, with dead zones at the ends, and forcing it past its end stop can break the wiper.

spans.text: An
incremental rotary encoder

outputs two square waves, A and B, offset slightly in timing. Counting the edges tells you how far the shaft has turned, and which channel leads tells you the direction. It reports change, not absolute position, so it forgets where it is when power is lost.

spans.text: Mechanical encoders chatter as their contacts close, an effect called bounce, which causes missed or extra counts unless you filter it in hardware or software.

blocks.caption: Encoder channels A and B. Count the edges for distance; which channel leads gives direction.

spans.text: A
limit switch

gives a plain on/off signal when something reaches the end of its travel. Configure a pull-up or pull-down resistor, or the input will float and read random values. It also bounces for a few milliseconds when it closes, so debounce it before counting presses.

spans.text: Hall effect sensors

respond to magnetic fields. The A3144 is a digital type that switches when a magnet comes close, and it usually responds to one magnetic pole. Its output can only pull low, so it needs a pull-up resistor to produce a clean high. The SS49E is a linear type with an analog output that sits around the middle of its supply with no magnet and moves up or down with field strength and polarity. A magnet on a rotating shaft with a Hall sensor beside it is a common way to measure speed.

Force

spans.text: A
force-sensitive resistor

, or FSR, drops in resistance as pressure rises. It is good for answering “was it pressed, and roughly how hard?” It is a poor weighing scale, because its response is not linear and varies with how the force is spread across it, with temperature, and over time.

blocks.text: A force-sensitive resistor, or FSR, drops in resistance as pressure rises. It is good for answering “was it pressed, and roughly how hard?” It is a poor weighing scale, because its response is not linear and varies with how the force is spread across it, with temperature, and over time.

spans.text: A
load cell

is a metal bar carrying strain gauges that change resistance very slightly when it bends. That change is far too small to read directly, so a load cell is paired with an amplifier chip, the HX711 being the common one, which has a 24-bit ADC and sends digital data over its own two-wire interface. Despite having a clock pin and a data pin, it is not I2C or SPI, so you need code written for it. Mounting matters, too. The load cell must be able to flex, so fix one end and leave a gap beneath the free end, or you will read zero. Load cells come rated for different capacities, from 1 kg to hundreds of kilograms, and are the standard choice for weighing.

Choosing a sensor

spans.text: Start with the quantity. Then check the range you need. Then match the output to what your controller can read: does it have an ADC, what logic voltage does it use, and how many free pins? Finally, read the datasheet for the exact part, as you learned in Topic 2.4.

spans.text: Consider a conveyor that must stop when a box reaches the end. You only need a yes or no, so a digital on/off sensor is enough, such as a limit switch or a distance sensor with a set threshold. If instead you need to know where the box is along the belt, an encoder on the belt motor counts how far the belt has moved, which tells you the position.

Where this leaves you

spans.text: You can now sort almost any sensor into a family by what it measures and into a signal type by what it outputs. You know the wiring traps that damage hardware or silently ruin readings: a missing pull-up, a 5 V echo on a 3.3 V pin, a gyroscope that drifts, a load cell mounted flat. Next comes Topic 3.3, where we connect these to a microcontroller and write the code that reads an analog voltage, a digital pin and an I2C sensor.

Analog signals: reading an LM35

spans.text: Connect the LM35's supply pin to 5 V, its ground pin to GND, and its output pin to analog input A0. Check the pin order in the datasheet, which is the skill from Topic 2.4, because wiring it backwards will heat the chip.

returns a whole number from 0 to 1,023, which is the ADC from Topic 3.1. This is the same worked example you saw there. At 35.0 °C the sensor outputs 0.350 V,

returns 71, the conversion gives 0.347 V, and the sketch prints 34.7 °C. Each ADC step here equals about 0.49 °C, so the readings move in half-degree jumps. That is the resolution limit, not a fault.

blocks.text: Digital data: I2C sensors

spans.text: I2C sensors share two wires, SDA for data and SCL for the clock, and every device on the bus has its own address. On the Uno, SDA is pin A4 and SCL is pin A5. Power and ground go to the sensor as usual. Before you read anything, scan the bus to confirm the sensor is actually there. This catches wiring mistakes in seconds.

spans.text: A BH1750 shows up at 0x23, or 0x5C if its address pin is pulled high. The BH1750 chip itself is a 3.3 V part, as you saw in Topic 3.2, so make sure your breakout board handles that before you connect it to 5 V. With the address confirmed, reading it takes a short sequence: send a command that starts measuring, wait, then ask for two bytes and join them into one number.

spans.text: Confirm the command byte and the divide-by-1.2 factor against the BH1750 datasheet for your own part, because a wrong command gives silence or nonsense. In practice, most people read I2C and other protocol sensors through a library, which hides these byte-level details. The DS18B20 from Topic 3.2, for example, is normally read through the OneWire and DallasTemperature libraries, which you install from the Library Manager. A library does not remove the wiring rules, so the DS18B20 still needs its 4.7 kΩ pull-up.

Taming noise

spans.text: Even with a constant input, analog readings wobble by a count or two, because of the noise you met in Topic 3.1. The simplest fix is to take several readings and average them.

blocks.caption: Averaging 16 readings smooths the random wobble, at the cost of a slower response.

spans.text: Averaging 16 readings cuts random noise by roughly a factor of four, since it falls with the square root of the number of samples. It does nothing about a sensor that is consistently wrong, and it slows the response, which is the response-time trade-off from Topic 3.1. For a slow temperature signal that is a good bargain. For a fast vibration signal it is not.

blocks.text: What Is an Actuator?

spans.text: Module 3 gave your controller senses. It can now measure temperature, distance, light and force. But a controller that only senses is an expensive thermometer. To change anything in the world, it has to act, and the devices that do the acting are actuators.

blocks.text: Module 3 gave your controller senses. It can now measure temperature, distance, light and force. But a controller that only senses is an expensive thermometer. To change anything in the world, it has to act, and the devices that do the acting are actuators.

blocks.caption: A controller that only senses cannot change anything. Add an actuator and it can act.

blocks.text: What an actuator is

spans.text: An actuator converts energy, most often electrical, into physical action: motion, force, heat, light or sound. It is the mirror image of a sensor. A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal. An actuator turns an electrical signal into a physical effect. Between them sits the controller, and together they form the sense-think-act loop from Topic 3.1. This module is about the last link.

blocks.text: An actuator converts energy, most often electrical, into physical action: motion, force, heat, light or sound. It is the mirror image of a sensor. A sensor turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal. An actuator turns an electrical signal into a physical effect. Between them sits the controller, and together they form the sense-think-act loop from Topic 3.1. This module is about the last link.

blocks.caption: Sensor, controller, actuator: the sense-think-act loop. This module focuses on the actuator.

spans.text: The word covers a wide range of devices. A motor spinning a wheel is an actuator. So is a solenoid that pops open a door lock, a heating element in an oven, a pump pushing water through a pipe, and a pneumatic cylinder clamping a part on a factory line.

Why a controller pin cannot drive one

spans.text: Here is the first problem every beginner hits. A microcontroller pin is a signal source, not a power source. On an Uno-class board, a pin can supply around 20 mA at 5 V, and your own board's datasheet gives the exact limit. Compare that with the motor from Topic 2.4, which drew 250 mA while running and 900 mA when stalled. Even a small motor wants many times what a pin can give.

blocks.caption: A controller pin supplies tens of milliamps. A small motor needs hundreds. The figures are illustrative.

spans.text: Connect the two directly and one of them fails, and it is not the motor. The pin overheats and the controller can be damaged or destroyed. So a controller never powers an actuator itself. It controls something that does.

The drive chain

spans.text: The solution is a three-part chain, with a separate power supply.

blocks.text: The solution is a three-part chain, with a separate power supply.

spans.text: The
controller
sends a small control signal, a few milliamps at most.

spans.text: A
driver
receives that signal and switches or regulates a much larger current. The driver can be a single transistor from Module 2, a relay, or a dedicated motor-driver chip.

spans.text: The
actuator
receives that larger current from a power supply that is separate from the controller's pins.

spans.text: The controller and the driver's supply must share a common ground, the same rule you met in Topic 3.3, or the control signal has no reference and the driver behaves unpredictably. Topic 4.2 shows how to build this chain for a DC motor.

Where actuators get their energy

spans.text: Electric actuators
are the ones you will use in this course: motors, solenoids, heating elements and buzzers. They are easy to control from a controller and need only a power supply and a driver.

blocks.text: Electric actuators are the ones you will use in this course: motors, solenoids, heating elements and buzzers. They are easy to control from a controller and need only a power supply and a driver.

spans.text: Pneumatic actuators

run on compressed air. A common form is a cylinder with a piston that extends when air is let in through a valve. They are fast, simple and clean, which is why they are common in factory clamps and pick-and-place machines. Air is compressible, so they are poor at holding a position precisely in the middle of their stroke.

They are fast, simple and clean, which is why they are common in factory clamps and pick-and-place machines. Air is compressible, so they are poor at holding a position precisely in the middle of their stroke.

spans.text: Hydraulic actuators

work the same way but use pressurized liquid, usually oil. Liquid hardly compresses, so these produce very large forces and hold their position firmly. Excavator arms and presses use them. The cost is a pump, hoses and the risk of leaks.

blocks.caption: Three energy sources: electric, pneumatic and hydraulic.

spans.text: A controller drives both pneumatic and hydraulic actuators the same way: it switches a valve, usually through an electric driver.

spans.text: Actuators sort by what they produce.

DC motors, servo motors and stepper motors.

spans.text: Linear motion:
solenoids, linear actuators and pneumatic or hydraulic cylinders.

spans.text: Light and sound:
LEDs and buzzers, usually called output devices, though they follow the same chain.

spans.text: Two properties matter for anything that moves.
Force
is the push or pull, measured in newtons.
Torque

is the equivalent for rotation, a twisting force measured in newton-metres. A motor that can spin fast but cannot turn a heavy load is no use, so you always ask both how much and how fast. Gearing trades one for the other: a gearbox lowers speed and raises torque. Topic 4.2 returns to this.

Controlling an actuator

spans.text: There are three ways to control one.

blocks.text: There are three ways to control one.

spans.text: On and off.
A transistor or relay either passes current or does not. This is enough for a heater, a solenoid or a fan that only needs to run or stop.

blocks.text: On and off. A transistor or relay either passes current or does not. This is enough for a heater, a solenoid or a fan that only needs to run or stop.

spans.text: Variable.

To change a motor's speed, you vary the average power it receives. Controllers do this with PWM, which switches the supply on and off thousands of times per second. The fraction of time it is on, the duty cycle, sets the average power. At 50% duty, a motor behaves roughly as though it were running at half the voltage. Topic 4.2 covers PWM properly.

blocks.text: Variable. To change a motor's speed, you vary the average power it receives. Controllers do this with PWM, which switches the supply on and off thousands of times per second. The fraction of time it is on, the duty cycle, sets the average power. At 50% duty, a motor behaves roughly as though it were running at half the voltage. Topic 4.2 covers PWM properly.

spans.text: With feedback.

Open-loop control sends a command and hopes it worked. Closed-loop control adds a sensor that measures the result and feeds it back, so the controller can correct itself. A heater that runs for ten minutes regardless of temperature is open-loop. A heater that runs until a temperature sensor reads the target is closed-loop. Closed loops are more accurate and more robust to changing conditions, and they are why Modules 3 and 4 belong together.

blocks.text: Two hazards to know now

spans.text: Stall current.

A motor that is jammed or overloaded stops turning and draws far more current than it does when running, which is the 900 mA case from Topic 2.4. Choose your driver for the stall current, not the running current.

blocks.text: Stall current. A motor that is jammed or overloaded stops turning and draws far more current than it does when running, which is the 900 mA case from Topic 2.4. Choose your driver for the stall current, not the running current.

spans.text: Inductive kick.

Motors, solenoids and relay coils store energy in a magnetic field. When you cut their current suddenly, they push back with a voltage spike that can be several times the supply and can destroy a transistor. A diode connected across the coil gives that energy a safe path. This is a job for the diodes from Topic 2.3, and Topic 4.2 shows where to place one.

When you cut their current suddenly, they push back with a voltage spike that can be several times the supply and can destroy a transistor. A diode connected across the coil gives that energy a safe path. This is a job for the diodes from Topic 2.3, and Topic 4.2 shows where to place one.

spans.text: Keep your fingers clear of anything that moves, switch power off before changing wiring, and treat heating elements as hot even after they are off. Never use a relay to switch mains electricity unless you are trained and the parts are rated for it.

A worked example: a temperature-controlled fan

spans.text: Say you want a small cooling fan to switch on when a box gets too warm. The fan is a 12 V DC type that draws 150 mA. These figures are illustrative, not from a specific part.

blocks.text: Say you want a small cooling fan to switch on when a box gets too warm. The fan is a 12 V DC type that draws 150 mA. These figures are illustrative, not from a specific part.

spans.text: A controller pin gives about 20 mA at 5 V. The fan needs 7.5 times that current at a different voltage, so the pin cannot drive it directly. The chain looks like this. An LM35 reads the temperature. The controller compares it with a threshold of 30 °C. When it is exceeded, the controller sets a pin high. That pin feeds a transistor, which switches the fan on from a separate 12 V supply. A protection diode sits across the fan, and the controller and supply share ground. When the temperature drops, the pin goes low and the fan stops.

An LM35 reads the temperature. The controller compares it with a threshold of 30 °C. When it is exceeded, the controller sets a pin high. That pin feeds a transistor, which switches the fan on from a separate 12 V supply. A protection diode sits across the fan, and the controller and supply share ground. When the temperature drops, the pin goes low and the fan stops.

blocks.caption: The fan example as a block diagram. The exact transistor and diode wiring is built in Topic 4.2.

spans.text: One refinement. If the fan turns on at 30 °C and off at 30 °C, the noise from Topic 3.3 makes it flicker as the reading hovers around the threshold. The standard fix is to turn on at 30 °C and off at 28 °C. That gap is called hysteresis, and it is why a closed loop works smoothly instead of chattering.

Choosing an actuator

spans.text: Work through five questions. What motion or output do you need? How much force or torque, and at what speed? How precise must it be? What supply voltage and current does it need? What interface does it need from your controller?

spans.text: Take a gate that must push boxes off a conveyor. The push is short, fast and on or off, so a solenoid or a small pneumatic cylinder fits. If instead you need an arm that swings to a chosen angle, a servo fits. For a belt that must run continuously and know its position, a DC motor with an encoder fits.

ai-m1-t1.1.title: What is AI, ML, and Deep Learning

blocks.text: Lesson

spans.text: If you've spent any time around the word "AI" lately, you've probably heard it used to mean about five different things depending on who's talking. A marketer uses it to mean "smart software." A researcher uses it to mean something much narrower. Before you build anything, you need these terms pinned down precisely.

blocks.text: If you've spent any time around the word "AI" lately, you've probably heard it used to mean about five different things depending on who's talking. A marketer uses it to mean "smart software." A researcher uses it to mean something much narrower. Before you build anything, you need these terms pinned down precisely.

spans.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI)

is the broadest term. It refers to any system that performs tasks which would normally require human intelligence — recognizing a face, understanding a sentence, deciding where to move a robotic arm. AI is the goal category, not a specific technique. A simple chess-playing program from the 1990s that follows hand-coded rules is technically AI. So is a modern system that writes essays. They achieve "intelligent behavior" through completely different means.

blocks.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the broadest term. It refers to any system that performs tasks which would normally require human intelligence — recognizing a face, understanding a sentence, deciding where to move a robotic arm. AI is the goal category, not a specific technique. A simple chess-playing program from the 1990s that follows hand-coded rules is technically AI. So is a modern system that writes essays. They achieve "intelligent behavior" through completely different means.

blocks.caption: An early rule-based chess program — AI, but no learning involved.

spans.text: Machine Learning (ML)

is a subset of AI — specifically, AI achieved by learning patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed with rules. Instead of a human writing out "if the sensor reads above X, do Y," you give the system a large number of examples, and it works out the pattern itself. This shift is what made modern AI possible: rules written by humans don't scale to the complexity of real-world problems like image recognition or language, but patterns learned from thousands or millions of examples can.

blocks.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI — specifically, AI achieved by learning patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed with rules. Instead of a human writing out "if the sensor reads above X, do Y," you give the system a large number of examples, and it works out the pattern itself. This shift is what made modern AI possible: rules written by humans don't scale to the complexity of real-world problems like image recognition or language, but patterns learned from thousands or millions of examples can.

spans.text: Deep Learning (DL)

is a subset of ML — specifically, ML done using a structure called a neural network, loosely inspired by how neurons connect in a brain. "Deep" refers to having many layers of these connected units stacked on top of each other. Deep learning is what powers most of the AI systems getting attention right now — image recognition, large language models, generative design tools.

blocks.text: Deep Learning (DL) is a subset of ML — specifically, ML done using a structure called a neural network, loosely inspired by how neurons connect in a brain. "Deep" refers to having many layers of these connected units stacked on top of each other. Deep learning is what powers most of the AI systems getting attention right now — image recognition, large language models, generative design tools.

blocks.caption: A neural network: input layer, hidden layers, output layer.

spans.text: So the relationship is a set of nested boxes:
AI contains Machine Learning, which contains Deep
Learning.

blocks.text: So the relationship is a set of nested boxes: AI contains Machine Learning, which contains Deep Learning.

blocks.caption: The nested relationship between AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning.

spans.text: Every deep learning system is machine learning. Every machine learning system is AI. But not every AI system uses machine learning, and not every machine learning system uses deep learning — plenty of ML techniques, like decision trees or simple regression, aren't neural networks at all, and are often the better choice for smaller or more structured problems.

blocks.text: Every deep learning system is machine learning. Every machine learning system is AI. But not every AI system uses machine learning, and not every machine learning system uses deep learning — plenty of ML techniques, like decision trees or simple regression, aren't neural networks at all, and are often the better choice for smaller or more structured problems.
Why this distinction matters practically, not just academically

spans.text: If someone tells you "we're adding AI to this product," that sentence alone tells you almost nothing about how it works, how much data it needs, or how predictable its behavior will be. Those things depend entirely on which box you're actually in.

blocks.caption: Rule-based logic vs. patterns learned from data.

spans.text: A rule-based AI system is predictable and explainable — you can point to the exact line of logic that produced a decision. But it's brittle: it only handles situations the programmer thought of in advance.

blocks.text: A rule-based AI system is predictable and explainable — you can point to the exact line of logic that produced a decision. But it's brittle: it only handles situations the programmer thought of in advance.

spans.text: A machine learning system is more flexible and can handle situations no one explicitly anticipated — but it needs data to learn from, and its decisions are harder to fully explain, which matters a lot in engineering contexts where you need to trust a system's output.

blocks.text: A machine learning system is more flexible and can handle situations no one explicitly anticipated — but it needs data to learn from, and its decisions are harder to fully explain, which matters a lot in engineering contexts where you need to trust a system's output.

spans.text: A deep learning system is the most powerful and flexible of the three for complex, unstructured problems — images, language, sensor fusion — but it typically needs the most data, the most computing power, and is the hardest of the three to fully explain when it makes a decision.
